messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Optimizing chain()
parts:
So I'm working on some more vari's for quadratic forms on matrices and
an issue has come up which is a matter of style and optimization.

Consider a (scalar valued) function defined on matrices, f(A,B,C). So
far the pattern for vari's (eg, det, dot_product) has been that the
vari structure contains pointers to the vari's of A, B and C and the
constructor of the vari simply copies data around and computes the
value of the function. The chain function then uses the stored vari
pointers to propagate the adjoint information.

This is fine for the typical use case, differentiating lp__, but if we
start computing Jacobians it would be inefficient, as each call would
recompute df/d{A,B,C}. We can store these values, but that uses more
memory.

The question is, are we likely to be computing Jacobians often? I
seem to recall that being part of the design for higher order
derivatives but I'm very fuzzy on how all of that is going to fit
together.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Optimizing chain()
parts:
Jacobians of R^N -> R^M functions are most efficiently
computing using n forward-mode passes, each computing
dy_m/dx_n for all m in 1:M and a single n.

Hessians of an R^n -> R function get computed with
n forward + reverse passes.

Hessian-vector products are easier. As are directional
derivatives.

You can see all the code in agrad/autodiff.hpp

We haven't finished all the functions in forward mode,
but Peter's working on it and should have them done by
the end of the summer if not sooner.

We need most of the obscure ops in autodiff.hpp for
Michael's softabs metric-based RM-HMC.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Optimizing chain()
parts:
I think I see where you were going with this now.
I only answered the literal question.

There's actually a large literature, which I'm not
on top of, concerning how to partially evaluate the
expression graph to trade off memory, efficiency,
and re-use (for instance, if doing code generation).
This seems to involve a lot of graph algorithms on the
expression tree and *sparse* Jacobian evaluations of graph
fragments.

We do this by hand when we define new compound functions
(like log1m()) that have their gradients calculated.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Optimizing chain()
parts:
Exactly. For a single set of calls to chain (computing the gradient
of a scalar valued function) it doesn't matter because the (local)
gradients only get computed once but if there are multiple calls
(computing a Jacobian) then you end up recomputing the gradients for
each set of calls. At any rate, since it seems like we won't be doing
Jacobians with the reverse mode autodiff, I don't need to worry about
this too much.

Cheers,
Marcus
